questions.title: How exactly does the 'two-step reasoning' in the prompt prevent spurious correlations compared to standard CoT?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the core innovation of the prompt design in FeatLLM. The paper mentions dividing the inference into two steps: first inferring causal relationships based on general knowledge, and second deriving rules based on few-shot examples. Why is this separation necessary? Does this explicitly force the model to ignore features that don't align with its priors before looking at the data, or is it just a heuristic? How does this differ fundamentally from a standard Chain-of-Thought prompt that asks for reasoning in one go?

questions.title: Clarification on Equation 1: What happens if a rule evaluates to false for all samples?
questions.question_body: Looking at Section 3.2, specifically Equation 1 and the surrounding text, I see that new binary features are generated where $\mathbf{z}_k^i$ is 1 if a sample satisfies a rule for class $k$, and 0 otherwise. If an LLM generates a rule that is logically impossible (e.g., 'Age > 150') or simply never true for any sample in the dataset, that column will be all zeros. Since the model learns weights $\mathbf{w}_k$ via cross-entropy loss, will such a useless feature naturally get assigned a weight of zero, or does it cause numerical instability in the optimization? The paper mentions filtering rules with weights below 0.1, but doesn't discuss handling constant-zero features explicitly.

questions.title: Is 'Feature Bagging' here equivalent to Random Forest's bootstrap sampling of rows?
questions.question_body: The paper describes using 'feature bagging' and selecting subsets of features/instances for each trial to mitigate prompt size limits and improve robustness. I am confused about the exact mechanism: Are they resampling rows (instances) like standard bagging in Random Forests, or are they randomly dropping columns (features) from the input prompt sent to the LLM? Or perhaps both? If they drop columns, how does this help if the LLM needs to see all columns to understand context? I need clarification on what constitutes a 'trial' in their ensemble method versus a standard bootstrapping procedure.

questions.title: Why use a linear model with ReLU-like projection ($\max(\mathbf{w}, 0)$) instead of just counting satisfied rules?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2, after generating binary features from rules, they fit a linear model without bias but project weights into a positive subspace ($\max(\mathbf{w}_k, 0)$). Why not just sum the number of satisfied rules per class (which seems like what they describe as an initial idea)? Does forcing non-negative weights imply that satisfying *more* rules must always increase probability? What theoretical justification exists for this constraint over allowing negative weights (which would mean satisfying a rule decreases confidence)? Also, why exclude the bias term entirely?

questions.title: How does FeatLLM handle conflicting rules generated by different ensemble members?
questions.question_body: Since FeatLLM relies on an ensemble of LLM queries with randomized temperatures and demonstrations, it is inevitable that different trials will generate contradictory rules (e.g., Trial A says 'Rule X implies Class Y', while Trial B says 'Rule X implies NOT Class Y'). How does the final aggregation step resolve these conflicts mathematically? Does it rely solely on the weighted voting scheme derived from training data weights $\mathbf{w}$, or is there an explicit conflict resolution logic before fitting the linear model?
